interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a 1 m square filling with 1000 rows of 1000 small squares, so 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², when you zoom in with the prefix dial on mm.
interactive.title: Zoom into the unit
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture: one metre, drawn as a length, a square or a cube. A power dial picks which, 1 for the length, 2 for the square metre and 3 for the cubic metre. A prefix dial picks the small unit, cm or mm, and Zoom fills the metre with that small unit, drawing a corner in full and counting the rest. Under the picture a readout writes the small unit as a power of ten and raises the whole bracket to the dial's power. Screen 1 opens on the 1 m length with the prefix on cm, and Zoom fills it with 100 cm. Turning the power dial to 2 makes it a square metre, and the same 100 cm now runs along two sides, so it fills with 100 rows of 100 small squares, 10,000 cm². Screen 3 zooms in with mm: 1000 mm along each side, 1000 rows of 1000, with the first row lit to show that 1000 mm² is only a strip 1 mm wide along one edge, and the readout writes 10⁻³ m × 10⁻³ m = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², the numbers multiplied by adding their powers and m × m making m². Screen 5 turns the power dial to 3 with cm: 100 cm along each of three edges, 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 small cubes, and (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. Screen 7 puts a 2.5 mm² cable's cross-section on the readout: each mm² is 10⁻⁶ m², so 2.5 mm² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m². Screen 9 turns it round for a unit you divide by: a load of 1 newton on every square millimetre, and zooming out to the square metre shows 10⁶ of them, each carrying 1 N, so 1 N/mm² = 10⁶ N/m². Screens 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 show an idea, and screens 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 ask you to try it: square millimetres in a square metre, 1 cm² in m², 1 mm³ in m³, a 1.5 mm² cable in m², and 200 N/mm² in N/m². Screens 11 and 12 mix them: a 500 cm³ cylinder in m³, and a 0.0004 m² busbar in mm², checked against its 40 mm by 10 mm sides. A puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is drawn in red beside the right one, so you can see it used the length factor once, or went the wrong way.
interactive.ignores: A million small squares cannot all be drawn on a phone, so the zoom draws a corner in full and counts the rest. The units are exact by definition: 1 mm² is exactly 10⁻⁶ m². A measured cable or bar is never exactly its stated size, so a converted value is only as good as the measurement. The dial has only cm and mm, and every other prefix goes inside the power in the same way. The cable sizes, loads, cylinder and busbar are examples.

explain.text:
A prefix and its unit make one symbol, so a power on the unit powers the prefix too: 1 mm is 10⁻³ m, so 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m².[^1] Here is why. A square millimetre is a square 1 mm along each side, and its area is side times side, 1 mm × 1 mm. Each side is 10⁻³ m, a thousandth of a metre,[^10] so the area is 10⁻³ m × 10⁻³ m. Multiply the numbers and the units separately. The numbers are powers of the same base, so their indices add,[^17] and −3 add −3 makes −6, giving 10⁻⁶. The units multiply too, and m × m is m². So 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², a millionth of a square metre.

Zoom into a square metre and you can count it. Along one side 1000 mm fit, so the [[length factor]], how many small units fit along one metre, is 1000. The square fills with 1000 rows of 1000 small squares, so 1 m² = 1,000,000 mm², which is 10⁶ mm². You met the same count for 1 cm² = 100 mm² in Geometry fundamentals, 10 rows of 10; the zoom does it for any prefix. The length factor counts in two directions, across and down, so an area conversion squares it, and a cube adds a third direction, depth, so a volume conversion cubes it.[^2] Centi is 10⁻²,[^11] so 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³: 100 cm along each edge of a cubic metre, and 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 small cubes.

Two easy slips come from using the length factor only once. One says a square metre holds 1000 mm², when 1000 is only the count along one edge: 1000 mm² is the first row alone, a strip 1 mm wide, and 999 more rows are still to fill. The other reads cm² as a hundredth of a square metre, as if the centi sat outside the square. NIST's guide to the SI rules that out: the prefix and the unit are one inseparable symbol, and the power belongs to both.[^1] So 1 cm² is (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m². The rule holds for a negative power too,[^1] which is how a unit you divide by is written, as dividing is multiplying by one over. A load of 1 N/mm² is 1 newton on every square millimetre. Per mm² means dividing by 10⁻⁶ m². A negative power is one over,[^5] so 10⁻⁶ is one millionth, and dividing by a millionth multiplies by a million: 1 N/mm² = 10⁶ N/m². The zoom agrees: a square metre holds 10⁶ square millimetres, each carrying 1 N. Textbooks add that a newton per square metre is a pascal, so 1 N/mm² is 10⁶ Pa, and mega is 10⁶,[^11] so that is 1 MPa.

**A power on a unit takes its prefix with it, so an area conversion squares the length factor and a volume conversion cubes it: 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m² and 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³.[^1][^2]**

analogy.text: Tiling a wall 1 m by 1 m with 10 cm square tiles, you fit 10 tiles along the bottom, but you buy 100, not 10, because there are 10 rows of 10. The 10 along one edge is the length factor, and the wall's area needs it twice.
analogy.breaks: Real tiles leave grout gaps and get cut at the edges, so a tile count is rounded up, while 1 m² = 10,000 cm² is exact. And a tile count cannot show a unit you divide by, such as N/mm², where the factor lands on the other side and the number grows.

practice.text:
To convert a unit with a power:
- Write the small unit as a power of ten times the metre: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 cm = 10⁻² m.
- Put a bracket round the power of ten and the metre together, and raise the whole bracket to the unit's power: mm² = (10⁻³ m)².
- Multiply the indices out: (10⁻³)² = 10⁻³ × 10⁻³ = 10⁻⁶, so mm² = 10⁻⁶ m².
- Swap it into the value: 6 mm² = 6 × 10⁻⁶ m².
- Check the direction: going to a bigger unit, the number in front gets smaller. For a unit you divide by, such as N/mm², it is the other way round, because each bigger unit holds more of the load.

**Rule of thumb:** area squares the length factor and volume cubes it.[^2] From mm: mm² to m² is × 10⁻⁶ and mm³ to m³ is × 10⁻⁹. From cm: cm² to m² is × 10⁻⁴ and cm³ to m³ is × 10⁻⁶. Between the two, 1 cm² = 100 mm² and 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³. A unit you divide by flips it: per mm² to per m² is × 10⁶.

**Worked example:** Say a formula needs a 6 mm² conductor's cross-section in square metres, because its other lengths are in metres. 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², so 6 mm² = 6 × 10⁻⁶ m², which is 0.000006 m². The number got smaller because the square metre is the bigger unit. A 250 cm³ oil sample is 250 × (10⁻² m)³ = 250 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

**Common mistakes**
- Using the length factor once for an area: a square metre holds 1,000,000 mm², not 1000.
- Leaving the prefix outside the power: 1 cm² is 10⁻⁴ m², not 10⁻² m².
- Squaring for a volume: 1 cm³ is 10⁻⁶ m³, not 10⁻⁴ m³.
- Going the wrong way: 1.5 mm² is 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m², not 1.5 × 10⁶ m². A smaller unit needs more of them.
